'''Allen Joseph Bard''' (December 18, 1933 – February 11, 2024) was an American chemist.<ref name=scopus>{{Scopus id}}</ref> He was the Hackerman-Welch Regents Chair Professor and director of the Center for Electrochemistry at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref>[http://bard.cm.utexas.edu/styled-2/ Allen J. Bard Vita], retrieved December 12, 2013.</ref> Bard developed innovations such as the [[scanning electrochemical microscopy|scanning electrochemical microscope]], his co-discovery of [[electrochemiluminescence]], his key contributions to [[photoelectrochemistry]] of [[semiconductor]] [[electrodes]], and co-authoring a seminal textbook.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books/about/Electrochemical_Methods.html?id=kv56QgAACAAJ Electrochemical Methods: Fundamentals and Applications – Allen J. Bard, Larry R. Faulkner – Google Books<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Allen J. Bard was born in New York City on December 18, 1933. He attended the [[Bronx High School of Science]] and graduated from the [[City College of New York]] in 1955.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Bard|first=Allen J.|date=June 12, 2014|title=A Life in Electrochemistry|journal=Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=1–21|doi=10.1146/annurev-anchem-071213-020227|pmid=24849115 |issn=1936-1327|doi-access=free|bibcode=2014ARAC....7....1B }}</ref> He then attended [[Harvard University]], where he earned a Masters (1956) and a PhD (1958).<ref name=":0"/>

== Research and career ==
[[File:Allen Bard - National Medal of Science, 2011.webm|thumb|Bard speaking about his life and career.]]
In 1958, Bard began working at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] and continued there for his entire career. However, he took a sabbatical in 1973 and worked in the lab of [[Jean-Michel Savéant]]. He also spent a semester at the [[California Institute of Technology]] as a Sherman Mills Fairchild Scholar. He lectured at [[Cornell University]] for the spring term in 1987 as a Baker Lecturer. In 1988 he served as the Robert Burns Woodward visiting professor at Harvard University.

Bard published more than 1000 peer-reviewed research papers, 88 book chapters and other publications, and had more than 30 patents. He has written three books: ''Chemical Equilibrium; Electrochemical Methods – Fundamentals and Applications,'' and ''Integrated Chemical Systems: A Chemical Approach to Nanotechnology.'' The title, ''Electrochemical Methods – Fundamentals and Applications'', is the defining text on [[electrochemistry]] in English, and generally referred to as just "Bard." He was the chief editor of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Campus briefs |journal=The Alcalde |date=January–February 1987 |volume=75 |issue=3 |page=31 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6NYDAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA31 |issn=1535-993X|last1=Communications |first1=Emmis }}</ref>

The Center for Electrochemistry was founded in 2006 in order to create a cooperative and collaborative group between the different types of concentrations in electrochemistry.<ref>[http://cec.cm.utexas.edu/ Center for Electrochemistry at UT]</ref> Bard and his group were one of the original researchers to take advantage of electrochemistry to create light. The creation of light produced a sensitive method of analysis that can now be applied to a wide variety of biological and medical uses, including determining if an individual has an HIV and analyzing DNA. The Bard group also "applies electrochemical methods to the study of chemical problems, conducting investigations in electro-organic chemistry, photoelectrochemistry, electrogenerated chemiluminescence, and electroanalytical chemistry."

== Personal life and death ==
Bard was married to Fran Bard until her death in August 2016.<ref>{{cite news |title=Fran Bard |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/statesman/obituary.aspx?pid=181121653 |access-date=February 15, 2020 |work=Austin American-Statesman |date=August 19, 2016}}</ref> He died in Austin on February 11, 2024, at the age of 90.<ref>{{cite web |title=Obituary for Allen Joseph Bard |url=https://www.austinnaturalfunerals.com/obituaries/Allen-Bard-2/#!/Obituary |access-date=14 February 2024 |website=}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Among Bard's awards are the [[Priestley Medal]] in 2002,<ref>[http://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/8014/8014bard.html "Electrochemistry's Shining Light", C&EN, 80(14), 39 (April 8, 2002).]</ref> the 2004 [[Welch Award in Chemistry]]<ref> [https://cen.acs.org/articles/82/i20/ALLEN-BARD-WINS-2004-WELCH.html/ "Allen Bard Wins 2004 Welch Award",  May 17 2004]</ref> and the 2008 [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]].<ref>[http://www.utexas.edu/news/2008/01/23/chemistry_bard/ "For Creating New Field of Science, Texas Chemist Wins International Prize", January 23, 2008] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111216023727/http://www.utexas.edu/news/2008/01/23/chemistry_bard/ |date=December 16, 2011 }}, retrieved July 7, 2008.</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1990.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=https://www.amacad.org/sites/default/files/academy/multimedia/pdfs/publications/bookofmembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=February 7, 2022}}</ref>

On February 1, 2013, President [[Barack Obama]] presented Allen Bard with a [[National Medal of Science]] for Chemistry, alongside fellow UT-Austin academic [[John Goodenough]] who received the corresponding award for engineering.  "I am proud to honor these inspiring American innovators," Obama said. "They represent the ingenuity and imagination that has long made this nation great – and they remind us of the enormous impact a few good ideas can have when these creative qualities are unleashed in an entrepreneurial environment."<ref>{{cite news |title=Goodenough, Bard Win National Medals of Science |url=https://news.utexas.edu/2013/02/11/goodenough-bard-win-national-medals-of-science/ |access-date=February 7, 2022 |work=UT News |publisher=University of Texas |date=February 11, 2013 |ref=UT News}}</ref>

On January 13, 2014, Allen Bard was awarded the [[Enrico Fermi Award]] along with [[Andrew Sessler]].<ref>[http://energy.gov/articles/president-obama-names-scientists-bard-and-sessler-enrico-fermi-award-recipients "President Obama Names Scientists Bard and Sessler as Enrico Fermi Award Recipients"] DOE Press Release:  January 13, 2014.</ref> In 2019 he received the [[King Faisal International Prize]] in Chemistry.<ref>[https://kingfaisalprize.org/ King Faisal International Prize 2019]</ref>
 
[[The Electrochemical Society]] established the Allen J. Bard Award in 2013 to recognize distinguished contributions to electrochemical science.<ref>{{cite web|title=Society Awards|url=http://www.electrochem.org/awards/ecs/ecs_awards.htm#z|website=The Electrochemical Society|access-date=June 24, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721022447/http://www.electrochem.org/awards/ecs/ecs_awards.htm#z|archive-date=July 21, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Bard was awarded the ACS Fisher Award in Analytical Chemistry in 1984<ref>{{cite web|title=Biography of Allen J. Bard|url=https://nitum.wordpress.com/2012/09/27/biography-of-allen-j-bard/|access-date=October 5, 2017|date=September 27, 2012}}</ref> and the Charles N. Reilley Award in 1984. He was granted the Eastern Analytical Symposium Award in 1990.<ref>[http://bard.cm.utexas.edu/ The Bard Group at UT]</ref><ref>[http://www.utexas.edu/know/2013/02/11/goodenough-bard-win-national-medals-of-science/ "Goodenough, Bard Win National Medals of Science"]</ref>
